question: Statements by the founder of Intellexa about supplying Predator software to governments attest to the part played by Nea Dimokratia in the wiretapping scandal. The main culprit is EU ‘rule of law’ and the legitimacy of ‘no one [being] exempt from surveillance’, which is cofashioned/implemented by Greek governments.

Part of the reactionary framework (Regulation (EU) 2021/821) is the legalisation of the conditions for the production, trade in, distribution and export of Predator-type spyware and the institutionalisation of mass surveillance for reasons of ‘national security’. Over 100 000 confidentiality of communications waivers have been approved in one decade.

The headquarters of the Greek Communist Party’s central committee were bugged/wiretapped and the investigation has been buried, with capitalist parties bearing responsibility for this. Similar software is being distributed in the EU.

In the current context of military preparedness/complicity, there is an intensification of repression and of the inculcation of the concept of ‘the enemy people’ aimed at silencing any popular struggle. The Greek Government is attempting to cover up mass surveillance and indiscriminate tracking. How does the Commission view the EU’s responsibilities, given that: 1.
the founder of the Predator spyware company admits to selling spyware to governments and ‘law enforcement authorities’ in accordance with the EU’s legislative framework?

many governments, including Nea Dimokratia, are using this framework, for instance Regulation (EU) 2021/821, to trade in and use spyware with all that this entails for the rights, freedoms and protection of the personal data of the people in each Member State?
answer: EN E-001304/26 on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission's position is very clear: any attempts to illegally access data of citizens, including journalists, representatives of civil society and political opponents, is unacceptable.

The legal interception or surveillance of communications can take place in limited circumstances, such as the prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences and subject to strict conditions and safeguards. Furthermore, the data protection Law Enforcement Directive1 is also applicable when competent authorities process personal data for law enforcement purposes.

National supervisory authorities have effective powers to examine any allegations of misuse, and data processed can be subject to judicial review. The European Media Freedom Act includes specific safeguards against the use of spyware against journalists and their families. The respective provisions entered into application in August 2025.
1 Directive (EU) 2016/680 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of

natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by competent authorities for the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Council Framework Decision 2008/977/JHA, OJ L 119, 4
